• The use or operation of any portable generator which exceeds decibels levels of 70 dBA by any vehicle.
The standards which are used to consider if any of these violations have occurred include, but are not limited to, the following (LMCO 99.03):
• The volume of the noise
• The intensity of the noise
• The volume and intensity of background noise
• The proximity of the noise to a residential area, place of public accommodation (e.g., hotel, motel, inn, campground, etc.), healthcare facility, church, or school
• The nature and zoning of the area within which the noise emanates
• The density of inhabitation of the area within which the noise emanates.
• The time of day or night that the noise occurs
• The duration of the noise
• Whether the noise is recurrent, intermittent, or constant
12.24.4 EXEMPTIONS
The following uses and activities are exempt from the noise ordinance (LMCO 99.03):
• Noises originating or emanating from safety signals, warning devices, and emergency pressure relief valves.
• Noises resulting from any authorized emergency vehicle or law enforcement training facilities.
• Noises resulting from construction or demolition activities, provided such activities take place between 0700 and 2100 hours.
• Noises relating to the use of farm machinery for agricultural purposes in farming operations.
• Noises relating to the use of lawn mowers or other machinery for landscaping purposes between 0700 and 2100 hours.
• Noises originating or emanating from public recreational facilities, such as, but not limited to, fairgrounds, sports arenas, sports stadiums, amusement parks, racetracks, and other public amusement establishments.
• The operation of any aircraft in conformity with, or pursuant to, federal law, federal air regulations, and/or air traffic control instructions.
12.24.4 EXEMPTIONS (CONTINUED)
• Noises resulting from any and all transportation, flood control, utility company maintenance, and construction operations at any time on right-of-ways and noises from situations which may occur on private real property, including parking lots, deemed necessary to serve the best interest of the public and to protect the public's health and well-being. These operations include, but are not limited to, the following:
o Street or hard surface sweeping or cleaning; o Debris and limb removal; o The removal of downed wires; o Restoring electrical services; o Repairing traffic signals; o Unplugging sewers; o Snow removal; o House moving; o Vacuuming catch-basins; o The removal of damaged poles and vehicles; or o The repair of water hydrants and mains, gas lines, oil lines, or sewers.
• Noises from activities conducted on public parks or playgrounds and public or private school grounds, including, but not limited to, school athletic and school entertainment events.
• Noises from activities conducted on property owned or operated by civic, charitable, or religious organizations, including, but not limited to, neighborhood or church festivals and entertainment events.
• Noises from activities at festivals, entertainment events, parades, and public assemblies, provided that a valid permit has been obtained from Louisville Metro Government.
• Noises from activities at fireworks displays, provided that all of the necessary permits have been obtained.
• Noises from activities conducted on rights-of-way of the Metro Government, including, but not limited to, festivals and entertainment events, provided that all of the necessary permits have been obtained.
• Noises relating to the collection of refuse between 0600 and 2200 hours.
Animal complaints, such as loud barking, are not a violation of the noise ordinance and should be referred to Louisville Metro Animal Services (LMAS).
12.24.5 CITATIONS
Noise ordinance violations are civil violations. Officers citing an individual for a violation of LMCO Chapter 99 will complete a handwritten hardcopy Kentucky Uniform Citation in lieu of an eCitation. Therefore, if an officer is citing or arresting an individual for criminal offenses in addition to the noise ordinance violation, then they must complete a separate paper citation for the noise ordinance violation. Failure to do so will result in the dismissal of the noise ordinance violation. The use of an electronic citation (eCitation) for noise ordinance violations is prohibited.
12.24.5 CITATIONS (CONTINUED)
When issuing a citation for a noise ordinance violation, an officer will:
• Not include the noise ordinance violation on the same citation with other violations.
• Leave the “Violation Code” block blank.
• Write “LMCO 99” in the “Statute/Ordinance” block.
• Write “Noise Ordinance” or abbreviate “NO” in the “Charge” block.
• Verify that the most appropriate of the following listed descriptions is written in the “Probable Cause Narrative” section:
o 87058 Noise Ordinance (Non-Vehicle Noise) o 88057 Noise Pollution Ordinance o 88133 Noise Ordinance (Noise from Vehicle)
• Verify that the description of the offense (written in the Post-Arrest Complaint section) includes the necessary elements as outlined in LMCO Chapter 99. Specific information regarding the incident is required to support a violation of this ordinance.
• Leave the “Court Date,” “Court Time,” and “Court Location” blocks blank.
• Write “NO” for noise ordinance in the “Type” block below the Control Number.
• Provide the violator with a copy of the Noise Ordinance Citation Instruction Sheet for Violators and the pink copy of the Kentucky Uniform Citation. The Noise Ordinance Citation Instruction Sheet for Violators can be found on the LMPD Intranet. Click on the “Forms” link and double click on the “Instructions” folder.
Noise ordinance violation citations will be turned in to the citing officer’s commanding officer by the end of their tour of duty. If the officer is off-duty, the citation will be forwarded by the end of their next tour of duty. If the blue copy is illegible, officers will photocopy the original and attach the photocopy to the blue copy prior to forwarding.
Divisions/sections/units will forward all completed citations for violations of LMCO Chapter 99 to LMPD Records Management, located at 701 West Ormsby Avenue, Suite 001, who will then forward the appropriate copies to the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC), Attn: Noise Citations, located at 444 South 5th Street, Suite 202. The copy of the citation can be emailed to ABCEnforcementDL@louisville.gov.
Fines for noise on premises that have ABC licenses are much higher than Chapter 99 fines (Kentucky Revised Statute (KRS) 244.120). If a location has an active ABC license, please note this in the narrative and forward the citation to ABC.

sections.title: Threat Management
sections.text:
12.25 THREAT MANAGEMENT
12.25.1 POLICY
The Louisville Metro Police Department (LMPD) recognizes the importance of responding to any threats against facilities, including schools, churches, businesses, events, and high-profile individuals, including dignitaries, celebrities, and political figures. The LMPD’s Homeland Security Unit provides the department with a group of specially-trained officers who are responsible for responding to actual, or perceived, threats at locations with the potential of mass casualties. This policy outlines the procedures for responding to any actual, or perceived, threats against locations or individuals.
12.25.2 AUTHORITY
The Homeland Security Unit, along with the Joint Terrorism Task Force (JTTF), will work as the lead investigators within the jurisdictional boundaries of Louisville Metro. Depending on the nature and scope of a particular threat, the Homeland Security Unit may require assistance from other LMPD units. When performing functions as the lead investigators outside of the boundaries of Louisville Metro, all efforts will be made for the Homeland Security Unit to notify the appropriate law enforcement agencies within these areas. When the Homeland Security Unit is assisting federal or state agencies, the notification will be made by those agencies, unless the LMPD is requested to make contact.
12.25.3 SOURCES
The Homeland Security Unit derives its cases from a variety of sources. These may include, but are not limited to, the following:
• Direction of the Chief of Police, or their designee
• Division detective units
• Private businesses/industries
• Citizen calls
• Select public officials
• Real Time Crime Center (RTCC)
• Dignitary Protection Team (DPT)
• Jefferson County Public Schools (JCPS)
• Other law enforcement agencies
12.25.4 RESPONSE
When a call for service is dispatched to division personnel, the initial call will be investigated by the assigned officer(s). Once preliminary information is obtained and it is determined that the Homeland Security Unit needs to become involved, the division commander, or their designee, will be notified.
Reviewed 11/27/24
12.25.4 RESPONSE (CONTINUED)
The division commander, or their designee, will contact the Homeland Security Unit Commander, or their designee, and brief them on the facts of the case. Once the Homeland Security Unit Commander, or their designee, has been briefed, they will make the decision to either call out a Homeland Security Unit member immediately for after-hours investigation or assign a Homeland Security Unit member during the following shift.
12.25.5 THREAT SCREENING
The Homeland Security Unit will review cases involving any individual, event, or facility who becomes the victim of specific acts or behavior which have been determined to warrant the Homeland Security Unit’s response. Upon receiving a case that warrants the Homeland Security Unit’s response, the assigned Homeland Security Unit member will conduct an in-person interview with the victim(s) as soon as possible. During the initial interview, the assigned Homeland Security Unit member will consult with the Homeland Security Unit Commander to determine if the case will be handled by the Homeland Security Unit or referred back to the division for investigation.
12.25.6 THREAT INVESTIGATION
Current threat management cases are categorized into three (3) types of investigative levels:
• Active Cases: Ongoing investigations that require contact with the victim.
• Inactive Cases: Ongoing investigations that have decreased in activity, are determined to not be an active threat, or have been cleared by arrest.
• Information Cases: When Homeland Security Unit personnel receive information that does not meet the above criteria, information will be collected from the reporting party. The information obtained will be retained per the established Homeland Security Unit file retention policy.
An initial interview will take place to obtain the pertinent information involving the threat. The interview should include the victim(s), the person(s) making the report, and all witnesses to the threats. All interviews will be recorded for future investigative purposes and be conducted pursuant to SOP 8.25. Once the dynamics of the case become obvious, the following procedures will be followed:
• All scenes will be considered crime scenes and will adhere to SOP 8.36.
• All letters, notes, etc. will be retained as evidence (refer to SOP 11.2).
• If the threats were made, via texting or calling, the text or voicemail and relevant telephone company records will be obtained, via a search warrant or subpoena, if necessary.
• If the threats were made, via email, the original email and identifying information from the Internet Service Provider (ISP) will be obtained by a search warrant or subpoena, if necessary.
• If an assault has taken place, photographs will be obtained as soon as possible, in addition to any medical records, and provided to the proper investigative unit.
• Photographs will be obtained of property damage, vandalism, and all evidence. These photos will be entered into the Digital Evidence Management System (DEMS) (refer to SOP 4.26).
Reviewed 11/27/24
12.25.6 THREAT INVESTIGATION (CONTINUED)
• Any damage to federal, state, or local governmental property will be handled in accordance with SOP 7.8.
12.25.7 THREAT ASSESSMENT
The primary goal of a threat assessment is to prevent an attack on an individual, event, or facility. Information is gathered, facts are evaluated, and a determination is made as to whether a given individual, or individuals, pose a threat of violence to an individual, event, or facility. If the assessment indicates that there is a risk of violence to an individual, event, or facility, a plan will be implemented to manage, or reduce, the threat posed by the individual in that situation.
A productive threat assessment involves three (3) key functions:
• Evaluating the threat
• Identifying the individual(s) responsible for the threat
• Interviewing the individual(s) responsible for the threat, evaluating the information that is gathered, and communicating with, and utilizing, resources to mitigate the threat
The threat assessment is used to provide recommendations that maximize the protection of the target(s) of a threat while neutralizing the perpetrator(s) who are making the threat.
The LMPD will assess any reported threats against dignitaries, celebrities, public officials, events, and facilities (e.g., businesses, schools) located in Louisville Metro. The Homeland Security Unit will also act as an advisor to schools, churches, and businesses, when requested, to initiate a threat assessment site review to recommend security and safety improvements in order to reduce the likelihood of facility threats.
12.25.8 CONFIDENTIALITY
All information and movement regarding approved assessments or investigations will be kept confidential for security. This includes information on past, current, and future investigations.
Reviewed 11/27/24

sections.title: Narcotics Overdose Response
sections.text:
12.26 NARCOTICS OVERDOSE RESPONSE
12.26.1 POLICY (KACP 17.14a-b)
It is the policy of the Louisville Metro Police Department (LMPD) that all officers are trained in the recognition of suspected narcotics overdose victims and equipped with the necessary tools to render aid to those victims. The LMPD will acquire, distribute, provide, and maintain an adequate supply of medication and first aid equipment to support the emergency treatment of suspected narcotics overdose victims. For suspected opioid-based narcotics overdose victims, the LMPD will train all officers on the administration of Naloxone nasal spray.
12.26.2 PURPOSE
The purpose of this policy is to provide guidance regarding the administration of Naloxone, an overdose intervention drug. Deaths from opioid-based narcotics overdoses can be mitigated using Naloxone. Kentucky Revised Statute (KRS) 217.186 permits law enforcement officers to possess and administer Naloxone for opioid-based narcotics overdoses.
12.26.3 DEFINITIONS
Naloxone: A medication which reverses the toxic effects of opioids by competing with the presence of opiates in the brain. It is a drug that acts within seconds to minutes of administration. It is safe to carry and administer and is impossible to abuse. No potential harmful side effects have been identified. Naloxone can be administered in a variety of ways. Nasal spray is the LMPD’s preferred system for administering Naloxone to a suspected opioid overdose victim.
Officer Overdose Kit: A departmentally-issued black pouch containing two (2) doses of Naloxone nasal spray that can be worn on a duty belt, be affixed to external vest carriers, or stored within a departmental vehicle for deployment.
Opiates: Synthetic or natural substances, prescribed or illicit, that cause sedation or pain relief effects. Excessive levels of opiates depress vital bodily functions, such as respirations and maintaining consciousness. Prescription opiates typically appear in the form of pain medication, which include Hydrocodone, Oxycodone, Morphine, Hydromorphone, Fentanyl, Carfentanyl, etc. One of the most common illicit forms of an opiate is Heroin.
Opiate Overdose: A life-threatening effect of an opiate on the human body, often depressing the respiratory and central nervous systems, resulting in a decreased level of consciousness. An opiate overdose can be reversed if proper medical treatment is administered in a timely manner.
Opiate Overdose Symptoms: Individuals who are experiencing an opiate overdose may exhibit symptoms such as not breathing, blue lips and/or blue skin, a limp body, decreased heart rate, lack of consciousness, deep snoring/gurgling, unresponsiveness to external stimuli, and/or pale, clammy skin.
12.26.3 DEFINITIONS (CONTINUED)
Overdose Response Kit (ORK): A departmentally-issued red medical bag containing multiple doses of Naloxone nasal spray along with first aid and personal protective equipment (PPE).
12.26.4 NALOXONE ADMINISTRATION (KACP 17.14b-c)
When an officer arrives on the scene of a possible overdose, they will assess the individual for symptoms of an opiate overdose.
Once the officer suspects the presence of any opiate overdose symptoms, they will:
• Immediately request Emergency Medical Services (EMS);
• Utilize universal precautions to prevent exposure to potential bloodborne pathogens and other potentially infectious materials (OPIM);
• Provide appropriate airway and/or ventilator support, such as rescue breathing;
• Administer Naloxone nasal spray in accordance with the officer’s training;
• Place the patient in a recovery position, unless there is evidence of head or neck trauma; and
• Monitor the patient’s respirations.
Officers will not administer Naloxone nasal spray to patients under five (5) years of age or under 44 pounds (KACP 17.14g).
Officers should be aware that the rapid reversal of an opiate overdose may cause projectile vomiting and/or violent behavior.
If, after the officer administers Naloxone nasal spray, they have reasonable grounds to believe that the individual has a mental illness, is a danger to themselves or others, or is in immediate need of hospitalization and treatment, they will refer to SOP 12.11.
12.26.5 DISTRIBUTION (KACP 17.14b)
All officers are assigned an Officer Overdose Kit to possess while performing official law enforcement duties. The kit can either be worn on their person (e.g., on their duty belt or affixed to their external vest carrier) or stored within their departmental vehicle.
All patrol divisions and designated specialty units will be assigned ORKs to deploy, as necessary, during the performance of police duties.
Commanding officers will maintain an accountability log that indicates to whom the ORKs are assigned during an incident, detail, or shift. The Special Operations Division (SOD) will assign ORKs to officers during details when there is a high likelihood of drug use or accidental overdose.
The Officer Overdose Kits are to be carried during the duration of officers’ shifts and/or details. Officers will maintain two (2) doses of Naloxone nasal spray in their kit.
12.26.5 DISTRIBUTION (CONTINUED)
The zipper on each ORK will be sealed with a red plastic, break-away seal. If the seal is intact on the ORK, this will identify to the officer that all the required contents are present in the kit. If the seal is broken or missing, the officer will need to open the kit in order to verify that all of the necessary contents are present and serviceable. The following inventory of items will be maintained in each ORK:
• Five (5) individual doses of Naloxone nasal spray
• One (1) bag valve mask
• Three (3) sharps containers
• Eight (8) pairs of Nitrile gloves
12.26.6 REPORTING (KACP 17.14b, e)
If an officer administers Naloxone nasal spray while on the scene of a suspected opiate overdose, they will complete the e-Naloxone form in the Kentucky Open Portal Solution (KYOPS).
If an officer is exposed to the blood, body fluids, or OPIM of the overdose victim, officers will immediately notify their direct supervisor. The supervisor will have MetroSafe immediately page an LMPD Health and Safety Officer (HSO).
12.26.7 MAINTENANCE AND REPLACEMENT (KACP 17.14b, f)
Officers will make a reasonable effort to store their assigned Officer Overdose Kit and ORK within a temperature range of 68°F and 77°F. This will be done by storing the Officer Overdose Kits on their duty belt, affixed to their external vest carrier, or within their departmental vehicle for deployment. ORKs will be stored on racks unless they are deployed for duty, then the ORKs will be kept in the passenger compartment of the officer’s vehicle. The trunk of a departmental vehicle is not a suitable or allowable storage area for the ORKs.
If an officer uses their Naloxone nasal spray and/or any ORK contents, they will acquire replacements from the HSO MedVend machines. If any ORK bag and/or its contents need to be replaced for any other reason (e.g., lost, damaged, defective, etc.), the officer will acquire the needed replacement(s) from the HSO MedVend machines. If an officer has expired Naloxone nasal spray, they are to contact the LMPD HSO via LMPD Health and Safety Resupply, to make an exchange. Expired Naloxone nasal spray will be collected by the LMPD HSO and used for training.
12.26.8 TRAINING (KACP 17.14a)
On a biennial basis, training will be provided to all LMPD officers on the administration of Naloxone nasal spray.

sections.title: Small Unmanned Aircraft System
sections.text:
12.27 SMALL UNMANNED AIRCRAFT SYSTEM (SUAS)
12.27.1 PURPOSE
The purpose of this policy is to describe the flight operation, functions, licensing requirements, and privacy considerations of the Louisville Metro Police Department (LMPD) Small Unmanned Aircraft System (SUAS).
12.27.2 POLICY
The SUAS is utilized as a resource by the LMPD to protect lives, safeguard property, and detect danger that could not otherwise be seen. The SUAS may be used for search and rescue operations, to assist in the apprehension of fleeing suspects, for critical incidents, special event overwatch, and to assist in any task that can best be accomplished from the air in an effective and efficient manner. This policy is designed to minimize the risk to persons, property, and the aircraft during the operation of the SUAS, while continuing to safeguard the constitutional right to privacy of all persons in accordance with the Kentucky Revised Statutes (KRS) and federal law.
12.27.3 DEFINITIONS
Certification (Certificate) of Authorization (COA): Certificate given by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which grants permission to fly within specific boundaries and perimeters. Training flights cannot take place without a valid training and evaluation (T&E) period.
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA): The component of the United States (U.S.) Department of Transportation (DOT) that is responsible for access of the national airspace.
Flight Currency: The ongoing demonstration of a pilot’s proficiency and experience within a specific time frame.
Observer: The member who is responsible for spotting any aerial in-flight obstacles that the SUAS may encounter.
Remote Pilot-in-Command (RPIC): The member who is responsible for all SUAS flight operations and equipment on the ground.
Small Unmanned Aircraft System (SUAS): An aircraft, either fixed-wing or rotor-wing, used in law enforcement missions, which flies in the national airspace and is controlled by pilots on the ground. Per Code of Federal Regulation 14 (14 CFR Part 107), Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems, the SUAS must be registered with the FAA and have a gross weight of less than 55 lbs. The SUAS will be clearly marked.
12.27.4 OPERATIONAL AND SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS
The SUAS is assigned to the Technical Services Lieutenant. The SUAS will be stored at a predetermined secure location. Only FAA 14 CFR Part 107-certified and trained personnel may operate a SUAS. The LMPD may operate a SUAS under CFR 14 Part 107. A COA is only required for operations beyond the scope of 14 CFR Part 107 (e.g., beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) or public aircraft operation (PAO)).
The SUAS will only be operated by personnel who have been trained and certified in the operation of the system.
SUAS operations in controlled airspace require prior FAA authorization, obtained via the Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability (LAANC) (Aloft Air Control), or FAA DroneZone.
SUAS Unit pilots may only operate one (1) SUAS at a time. All operations will remain within the RPIC’s Visual Line of Sight (VLOS), using unaided vision (corrective lenses allowed), unless authorized by an approved FAA COA.
SUAS use is authorized for the following:
• Documentation of crime and vehicle collision scenes;
• Hazardous material (HAZMAT) incidents;
• Search and rescue operations;
• Barricaded subjects/Special Weapons and Tactics (SWAT) Team call-outs;
• Disaster responses;
• Searches for fleeing suspects;
• Active aggressor incidents;
• Training;
• Traffic control operations;
• Special event overwatch;
• In-progress incidents where a short-term aerial presence would be beneficial; and/or
• Any other incidents approved by the Chief of Police, or their designee;
SUAS use is prohibited for the following:
• To monitor protected activities, such as areas where a person would have a reasonable expectation of privacy, absent a search warrant or exigent circumstances;
• To target a person based solely on actual, or perceived, characteristics, such as race, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, economic status, age, cultural group, or disability;
• To harass, intimidate, or discriminate against any individual or group; and/or
• To conduct personal business, of any type.
Any complaints or allegations of civil violations of rights/civil liberties, or privacy, will be investigated through the proper chain of command.
12.27.4 OPERATIONAL AND SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS (CONTINUED)
RPICs must assess flight risks, including, but not limited to, the following:
• The weather;
• Failure modes;
• Personnel fitness;
• Airspace;
• Equipment reliability; and
• Communication requirements.
The RPIC is authorized to refuse any flight request based on their assessment of the flight risks, any other safety concerns, or the legality of the flight.
While the SUAS is in flight, the RPIC is authorized and is responsible for making all decisions regarding the use of the SUAS, including, but not limited to, the following:
• Direction of the SUAS;
• Duration of the flight time;
• Capabilities of the SUAS;
• Maximum load allowance;
• Use of affixed certified equipment;
• Allowance or advisability of affixing additional personal or departmental equipment; and
• Configurations.
RPIC and Observer duties include, but are not limited to, the following:
• Maintaining a current FAA Unmanned Aircraft Operator Certificate, completing a biennial flight review, and successfully passing a recurrent aeronautical knowledge test for an RPIC holding an Unmanned Aircraft Operator Certificate.
• Maintaining current awareness of all pertinent SUAS agency requirements, FAA regulations, and other SUAS regulatory data bearing on the performance of their duties.
• Flight planning and preparation, including preflight inspections of the SUAS, and its equipment, in addition to a weather briefing.
• Performing overwatch in support of SWAT Team operations.
• Flight operations, including course, air speed, altitude and duration, landing zone selection, minimum flight approvals, and landing judgments with regards to weather or other criteria.
• Monitoring all Very High Frequency (VHF) air-to-air, air-to-ground, ATC, and any other radio communications.
• Timely reporting of new or previously unknown hazards that are encountered.
• Post-flight hardware inspection, including a verification that the batteries are recharged, video has been uploaded/categorized, flight logging for each flight, and the SUAS is ready for the next mission.
12.27.5 FLIGHT OPERATIONS AND OPERATIONAL CONTROL
There will only be one (1) RPIC for a single SUAS, at any given time, and they will exercise final responsibility and authority for the safety of the SUAS, personnel, and equipment during flight operations.
Prior to any flight, the RPIC is responsible for pre-flight inspections of the aircraft according to the pre-flight checklist. Any issues found by the RPIC will be fixed before a flight is conducted. A post-flight inspection will be conducted by the RPIC according to the post-flight checklist after each flight. Emergency deviations are permitted for safety. Notice to Airmens (NOTAMs) may be used if they are required by the FAA, or for emergency flights under a COA but are not required for routine 14 CFR Part 107 operations.
There will be a checklist for each phase of flight, including, but not limited to, the following:
• Pre-flight hardware inspection.
• Initiating the flight only when they are confident that the flight can be conducted safely.
• Verifying that an FAA NOTAM is released for every flight involving the SUAS in the national airspace.
• Verifying that there is a COA from the FAA to conduct flights in the national airspace.
• Reviewing a search warrant if a search warrant is required to fly the SUAS during a deployment.
• The landing.
• A post-flight hardware inspection.
The RPIC will not deviate from the checklist, unless otherwise instructed by the SUAS Unit Supervisor. The SUAS Unit Supervisor is responsible for making sure all checklists are up-to-date.
In the event of an emergency involving the safety of persons or property, the RPIC may deviate from the procedures of this directive relating to aircraft, equipment, and weather conditions to the extent required during the emergency.
The Observer has the following authority:
• They are responsible for see-and-avoid operations of the aircraft. The Observer will maintain contact with the RPIC and communicate any obstacles that the SUAS may encounter.
• When the flight becomes a hazard to ground personnel or other aircraft, the Observer will immediately notify the RPIC.
• During any phase of the flight, if the Observer notices a malfunction with the SUAS, they will notify the RPIC, who will immediately terminate the flight.
• They are responsible for all radio communications with ATC and MetroSafe.
• They are responsible for the law enforcement aspect of the deployment.
• They will operate any attachments to the SUAS, allowing the RPIC to maintain a complete focus on the operation of the SUAS.
Incidents resulting in serious physical injury or property damage will be reported immediately to the FAA within ten (10) days.
12.27.6 TRAINING REQUIREMENTS
All RPICs will hold a current FAA Unmanned Aircraft Operator Certificate and meet training requirements and annual reviews, as outlined in the SUAS Unit Operations Manual. Flight currency must be maintained. Personnel who are inactive for over 90 days, or longer, will not serve as RPICs or Observers without retraining. The Technical Services Supervisor is responsible for maintaining standardization and recurrent evaluations.
12.27.7 PRIVACY
The SUAS will not be used for general investigative surveillance. RPICs must avoid the unnecessary recording of uninvolved individuals to safeguard public privacy. All operations will comply with federal, state, and local privacy laws. Recordings and logs will be reviewed by the Technical Services Lieutenant or SUAS Unit Supervisor.
12.27.8 IMAGE RETENTION AND DOCUMENTATION
All SUAS video and imagery will be uploaded to evidence.com, post-mission and retained according to applicable records retention schedules. Flight logs will document flight dates, times, locations, purposes, and dispositions. Flight-time counters are maintained and reset only by the RPIC, with command approval. Regular, random audits and monitoring of flights will be conducted to verify that the SUAS is being utilized pursuant to the procedures outlined in the department’s Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs). Recordings and flight logs will be reviewed by the Technical Services Lieutenant or SUAS Unit Supervisor.
12.27.9 DISTRIBUTION OF RECORDINGS TO OUTSIDE AGENCIES OR PERSONS
Recordings generated on departmentally-owned equipment are the property of the LMPD. Copying or reproducing any recording, or segment of any recording, generated by the LMPD, or the removal of any recording outside of the LMPD, without the written authorization of the Chief of Police, or their designee (Deputy Chief of Police or Assistant Chief of Police), is prohibited.
Open records requests for copies of recordings, from persons or agencies outside of the LMPD, will be directed to Open Records at the following link: https://louisvillemetrogov-ky.nextrequest.com/. Open records requests submitted to Open Records by the media will be directed to the Media and Public Relations Office (refer to SOP 3.3) (KACP 20.2b). Any parts of a recording that infringe on an individual’s privacy rights or may compromise an investigation may be redacted.
Any member of the LMPD may request a copy of a SUAS recording from LMPD Video Records by emailing a completed Video System Request form (LMPD #15-0013) to “LMPD Video System Request,” located within the department’s email distribution list.
Recordings provided to persons or agencies outside of the LMPD will be duplicated on discs and will be provided by the department for a reasonable fee. The unauthorized duplication of recordings is prohibited.
Only the portion of a recording which contains a specific contact in question may be reproduced.
12.27.9 DISTRIBUTION OF RECORDINGS TO OUTSIDE AGENCIES OR PERSONS (CONTINUED)
Nothing in this section prevents officers from securing, or releasing, copies of SUAS recordings to the United States Attorney’s Office, Jefferson County Attorney’s Office, or Office of the Commonwealth’s Attorney for official purposes.

sections.title: Clergy De-Escalation Unit
sections.text:
12.28 CLERGY DE-ESCALATION UNIT
12.28.1 POLICY
The Louisville Metro Police Department (LMPD) recognizes the trauma violence inflicts on our communities. While crime scene integrity must always be preserved, the presence of trusted clergy members can be beneficial in de-escalating emotionally-charged events. The utilization of a clergy-based de-escalation response can alleviate tensions and open lines of communication in other situations, such as officer involved critical incidents.
12.28.2 PURPOSE
The purpose of this policy is to provide procedures regarding the activation of the Clergy De-Escalation Unit.
12.28.3 DEFINITIONS
Clergy De-Escalation Unit: Unit comprised of local clergy who respond to incident scenes and assist in crowd de-escalation. Situations that may require a clergy de-escalation response include, but are not limited to, homicide scenes, civil disturbances/disorderly crowds, critical incidents, and any other incident an on-scene commander may deem a de-escalation response would be beneficial. Members of the Clergy De-Escalation Unit report to the Community Engagement Unit commander.
12.28.4 RESPONSE
The request for the Clergy De-Escalation Unit will come from an on-scene commander and a notification will be sent through the Community Engagement Unit Commander, or their designee. The Clergy De-Escalation Unit will report to the on-scene commander and assess the needs of the scene and locations for deployment. The Clergy De-Escalation Unit will be easily identifiable by Chaplain polo shirts or vests clearly marked as “Clergy De-Escalation Unit.” These members will also have an LMPD-issued photo identification (ID).
The incident commander (IC) will designate a separate perimeter outside of the crime scene’s outer perimeter to which the Clergy De-Escalation Unit may respond. At no time will a Clergy De-Escalation Unit member enter the outer perimeter tape without the consent and escort of an on-scene commander, or their designee. Nothing in this policy prevents an on-scene commander from restricting perimeter access to any member of the Clergy De- Escalation Unit. The on-scene commander will have authoritative control over the scene and responding members of the Clergy De-Escalation Unit will serve at the direction of the on-scene commander. When practical, Clergy De-Escalation Unit members will be allowed to speak with members of the crowd in order to de-escalate the situation.
The Community Engagement Unit Commander, or their designee, is responsible for the training, recruitment, outfitting, and retention of the Clergy De-Escalation Unit members. An After-Action Report (LMPD #08-0005) will be completed by the Community Engagement Unit Commander and forwarded, through the chain of command, to the appropriate Bureau Commander for all incidents where Clergy De-Escalation Units were utilized.
Reviewed 08/02/23
12.28.4 RESPONSE (CONTINUED)
Clergy De-Escalation Unit members may also be utilized during the Community and Police Response to Victim’s of Violence (CPRVV) notifications. When utilized in these situations, the Clergy De-Escalation Unit members will report to the direction of the LMPD CPRVV Notification Commander who is present.
Reviewed 08/02/23

sections.title: Dispersal Orders
sections.text:
12.29 DISPERSAL ORDERS
12.29.1 PURPOSE
The purpose of this policy is to provide guidance regarding the issuing of dispersal orders during civil disturbance and crowd management situations (also refer to SOP 12.6).
12.29.2 DEFINITIONS
Civil Disturbance: An unlawful assembly that constitutes a breach of the peace or any assembly of persons where there is imminent danger of collective violence, destruction of property, or other unlawful acts (refer to Kentucky Revised Statute (KRS) 525.050) (refer to SOP 12.6).
12.29.3 DISPERSAL ORDER FORMAT
The following dispersal order format is included for reference and is to be used by the Louisville Metro Police Department (LMPD) when preparing to disperse crowds and prior to effecting any arrests related to unlawful mass demonstrations (i.e. civil disturbances/disorderly crowds) (refer to SOP 12.6).
Dispersal order warnings should be given with a bullhorn, a public address (PA) system, or Long-Range Acoustic Device (LRAD), preferably by the Incident Commander (IC), or their designee, in a loud and clear manner (KACP 17.4). When feasible, an officer who is staged at a safe vantage point away from the sound amplification device should record the warning on their Body-Worn Camera (BWC) and confirm to the officer who is giving the dispersal orders that they were audible and clear. A route of egress must be provided when making the announcement(s) with as much specificity as possible.
The official dispersal order to be utilized is as follows:
• I am (rank/name), a sworn police officer for the Louisville Metro Police Department.
• I hereby declare this activity to be unlawful and command all of those who are assembled here to immediately leave.
• If you do not do so, you may be arrested or subject to other police action.
• If you remain in the area, regardless of your purpose, you will be in violation of Kentucky law.
• The following routes of dispersal are available (describe available direction for exit). You have _____ minutes to leave. If you refuse to move, you will be arrested.
• This is your (first/second) warning.
• (ADD TO LAST WARNING ONLY) This is your final warning.
In order to document all dispersal orders, the officer will notify MetroSafe after each warning is given and provide times, locations, the officer’s code number, and direction of egress (KACP 19.2l).
Reviewed 12/09/24
12.29.4 DISPERSAL ORDER WARNING NOTIFICATION PROCEDURE (KACP 19.2l)
First warning:
• Provide MetroSafe with the:
o Time the dispersal order was given. o Location. o Officer’s code number. o Direction of egress provided. o Confirmation of first warning.
• Wait five (5) minutes before reading the second warning.
Second Warning:
• Provide MetroSafe with the:
o Time the dispersal order was given. o Location. o Officer’s code number. o Direction of egress provided. o Confirmation of second warning.
• Wait five (5) minutes before reading the third warning.
Third Warning:
• Provide MetroSafe with the:
o Time the dispersal order was given. o Location. o Officer’s code number. o Direction of egress provided. o Confirmation of third/final warning.
• Commence making arrests.
When feasible, the five (5)-minute interval between warnings will be utilized. However, based on the severity of the crowd’s behavior, the five (5)-minute interval between warnings may be reduced to a one (1)-minute interval, if necessary. More than three (3) warnings may be given or time may be extended when the crowd has displayed clear attempts to comply with orders.
12.29.5 IMMEDIATE ENFORCEMENT/ACTION
If, at any point, the IC determines or receives information that grave danger or a risk of serious physical injury to officers or civilians exists, or destruction of property is imminent, the IC must notify MetroSafe of this
Reviewed 12/09/24
12.29.5 IMMEDIATE ENFORCEMENT/ACTION (CONTINUED)
development and commence with necessary immediate enforcement/action(s) to mitigate the danger(s) (KACP 17.4, 19.2l).
Reviewed 12/09/24

sections.title: Handle with Care Program
sections.text:
12.30 HANDLE WITH CARE PROGRAM
12.30.1 POLICY
The Handle with Care (HWC) program is a notification system identifying children who have been exposed to trauma at scenes of crimes or accidents. The premise of the HWC program is to mitigate the negative effects of trauma on children (refer to https://www.kentuckystatepolice.ky.gov/handlewithcare). It Is the policy of the Louisville Metro Police Department (LMPD) to participate in the Handle with Care (HWC) program in partnership with the Kentucky State Police (KSP) (refer to Kentucky Revised Statute (KRS) 16.128).
12.30.2 PROCEDURES
An HWC notification will be completed when any child, who is under the age of 18, experiences a traumatic event at home or in their community. The following is the only information provided with an HWC notification:
• Child’s name;
• Child’s school;
• Child’s grade; and
• Child’s age.
HWC notifications are confidential and exclude all details of the traumatic event experienced by the child. Notifications will be initiated year-round, including periods where school or childcare providers are not in session (e.g., summer break or holidays).
Traumatic events include, but are not limited to, events where the child:
• Is a victim of a crime;
• Witnesses a crime (e.g., homicide, fatal accident, suicide, overdose);
• Experiences the loss of a caregiver or family member to a fatality or a mental health call for service;
• Is threatened with death or serious bodily injury;
• Experiences family disturbances;
• Becomes a victim, or suspected victim, of a physical or sexual assault;
• Is being removed from their place of residency or the custody of their guardians; or
• Is present during the execution of a warrant, during the arrest of parents, guardians, caregivers, or family members, or during the service of an order of protection in which a child is named.
The HWC notification system is located on the homepage of the Kentucky Open Portal Solution (KYOPS). A list of schools and childcare providers is located in the KYOPS, and in the event the child’s provider is not listed, the officer who is completing the notification will contact the KSP, via email, at danielle.perkins@ky.gov.
12.30.3 OFFICER RESPONSIBILITIES
The officer who responds to a traumatic event will identify all children, to include the friends of the children or witnesses who are under the age of 18, who are potentially exposed to the traumatic event and initiate an HWC notification through the KYOPS. If the child is present during the traumatic event and the officer believes there is an imminent threat, they will then take custody of the child, per KRS 620.040. Any arrests, to include
12.30.3 OFFICER RESPONSIBILITIES (CONTINUED)
handcuffing or questioning, will be made in a location outside of the child’s view, when reasonable. If necessary, the officer will explain the circumstances of the traumatic event to the child in an age and developmentally- appropriate manner. If necessary, the officer may involve the Victim Services Unit (VSU) for emotional support of the child or other involved persons.
The HWC notification system will be utilized by officers in addition to all required LMPD forms for calls for service. If the event requires the completion of a JC-3 form, the officer who is in charge will initiate an HWC notification. All HWC notifications will be completed prior to the following day that the child returns to school or childcare.
12.30.4 VICTIM SERVICES UNIT (VSU) RESPONSIBILITIES
If a Victim Services Specialist is on-scene at the time of the traumatic event or responds to an associated location, the Victim Services Specialist will coordinate with law enforcement to ensure an HWC notification is completed.

sections.title: Property Nuisance Abatement
sections.text:
12.31 PROPERTY NUISANCE ABATEMENT
12.31.1 OVERVIEW
It is the policy of the Louisville Metro Police Department (LMPD) to aid Louisville Metro Government (LMG), including the Department of Codes and Regulations, with property nuisance abatement (refer to Kentucky Revised Statutes (KRS) 65.8801).
12.31.2 TYPES OF PROPERTY NUISANCE ABATEMENT
The Division Resource Officers (DROs) will serve as the point-of-contact between the LMPD and the Department of Codes and Regulations for nuisance abatement and nuisance properties (refer to SOP 1.11). While DROs are the main point-of-contact, any officer may be requested to assist if DROs are unavailable.
In general, there are four (4) types of property nuisance abatements in which the LMPD will aid LMG:
• Imminent Danger (Louisville Metro Code of Ordinances (LMCO) 156.806) (e.g., gas line breaks, fires, and partial or full collapse of structures);
• Condemned and Emergency Boarding (CEB) (LMCO 156.805) (pink sticker) (e.g., boardings and may include other abatements, if deemed necessary by the Department of Codes and Regulations);
• Jefferson County Court-Ordered Nuisance Abatements (CONAs) (e.g., boardings and cleanings); and
• Vacant and Abandoned Properties (VAPs) (e.g., boardings and cleanings).
Imminent danger is the only type of property nuisance abatement that does not require documentation.
12.31.3 PROCEDURES
The LMPD does not assist when a property has only been ordered to vacate by the Department of Codes and Regulations unless they have a public safety reason to request police assistance. If requested for a public safety reason to assist, and LMPD officer may only enter under the following circumstances:
• Exigent circumstances;
• A search warrant;
• Consent; and/or
• Plain view doctrine:
o Lawful vantage point. o Incriminating nature – immediately apparent. o Lawful right of access.
DROs will be contacted, via email, by the Department of Codes and Regulations for CONA, VAP, or CEB property nuisance abatements. DROs will enter the initial information and paperwork into the LMPD Property Nuisance Abatement Smartsheet, and coordinate scheduling a mutually agreed-upon date/time to aid LMG with property nuisance abatement. If DROs are unavailable for an emergency issue, patrol officers may be requested to assist. If they are requested to assist, the patrol officers should send correspondence to the division DRO, including the date, time, and address, so that the DRO can input that information into the Smartsheet.
12.31.3 PROCEDURES (CONTINUED)
Prior to arriving at the property for nuisance abatement, DROs will prepare, including reviewing any required paperwork, a team which, at minimum, will include two (2) officers. DROs will also notify MetroSafe.
Regardless of any law enforcement actions (i.e., arrest), when a property has been cleared for approved nuisance abatement, a DRO will remain at the property to assess if continued LMPD resources are necessary to aid LMG.
DROs are also responsible for updating the LMPD Property Nuisance Abatement Smartsheet, prior to the end of their shift, when aiding LMG with a CONA, VAP, or CEB.
LMPD officers are to enforce the laws on CONA, VAP, or CEB properties when:
• Initially clearing the property/structures for approved LMG property nuisance abatement.
• Thereafter, including, but not limited to, when persons have clearly damaged the boarding to illegally enter the properties/structures; and
• If a DRO is unavailable and an immediate CONA, VAP, or CEV is necessary. Officers will assist with the nuisance abatement and then send pertinent information to the DRO for entry into the Smartsheet.
When a DRO or patrol officer is concerned with the request for assistance, they may have their commanding officer review the request and determine if the LMPD will assist.
